The schooner '''''Clotilda''''' (often misspelled ''Clotilde'') was the last known U.S. [[slave ship]] to bring enslaved individuals from [[West Africa|West]] and [[Central Africa]] to the United States, arriving at [[Mobile Bay]], in autumn 1859<ref name=FerrisJMC/> or on July 9, 1860,<!--see talk page--><ref name=SoulA/><ref name="LOCAT">{{cite web |title=AfricaTown, USA |url=http://lcweb2.loc.gov/diglib/legacies/AL/200002671.html |work=The American Folklife Center: Local Legacies |publisher=The Library of Congress | access-date=2009-05-12}}</ref> with 110 African men, women, and children.<ref name="Raines_p69">{{cite book |last1=Raines |first1=Ben |title=The Last Slave Ship: The True Story of How Clotilda Was Found, Her Descendants, and an Extraordinary Reckoning |date=2022 |publisher=Simon & Schuster |location=New York, NY |isbn=9781982136048 |page=69}}</ref> The ship was a two-masted [[schooner]], {{convert|86|ft|m}} long with a [[Beam (nautical)|beam]] of {{convert|23|ft|m|abbr=on}}.

U.S. involvement in the [[Atlantic slave trade]] had been banned by [[United States Congress|Congress]] through the [[Act Prohibiting Importation of Slaves]] enacted on March 2, 1807 (effective January 1, 1808), but the [[post-1808 importation of slaves to the United States|practice continued illegally]]. In the case of the ''Clotilda'', the voyage's sponsors were based in the South and planned to buy Africans in [[Ouidah|Whydah]], [[Dahomey]].<ref name="FerrisJMC">David Pilgrim. "[https://ferris.edu/HTMLS/news/jimcrow/question/2005/july.htm Question of the Month: Cudjo Lewis: Last African Slave in the U.S.?]" Jim Crow Museum, [[Ferris University]], July 2005.</ref><ref name="SoulA">"Black Travel - Soul Of America | Home" (historic sites), Soul of America, 2007, webpage: [https://www.soulofamerica.com/index.php?id=6678,1745,0,0,1,0 SoulofAmerica-6678].</ref> After the voyage, the ship was burned and [[Scuttling|scuttled]] in Mobile Bay in an attempt to destroy the evidence.

After the [[American Civil War|Civil War]], [[Cudjoe Lewis|Oluale Kossola]], also known as Cudjo Lewis,<ref name=FerrisJMC/> and 31 other formerly enslaved people founded [[Africatown]] on the north side of [[Mobile, Alabama]]. They were joined by other continental Africans and formed a community that continued to practice many of their West African traditions and [[Yoruba language]] for decades.

A spokesman for the community, Kossola lived until 1935 and was one of the last survivors from the ''Clotilda''. [[Redoshi]], another captive on the ''Clotilda'', was sold to a planter in [[Dallas County, Alabama]], where she became known also as Sally Smith. She married, had a daughter, and lived until 1937 in [[Bogue Chitto, Alabama|Bogue Chitto]]. She was long thought to have been the last survivor of the ''Clotilda''.<ref name="durkin">{{cite journal |title=Finding last middle passage survivor Sally 'Redoshi' Smith on the page and screen |last=Durkin |first=Hannah|journal=Slavery & Abolition |volume=40 |issue=4 |pages=631–658 |date=26 March 2019 |doi=10.1080/0144039X.2019.1596397 |s2cid=150975893 }}</ref> Research published in 2020 indicated that another survivor, [[Matilda McCrear]], lived until 1940.<ref name="Durkin 431–457">{{Cite journal|last=Durkin|first=Hannah|date=2020-03-19|title=Uncovering The Hidden Lives of Last Clotilda Survivor Matilda McCrear and Her Family|journal=Slavery & Abolition|volume=41|issue=3|pages=431–457|doi=10.1080/0144039X.2020.1741833|s2cid=216497607|issn=0144-039X}}</ref>

Some 100 descendants of the enslaved people carried by the ''Clotilda'' still live in Africatown, and others are around the country. After [[World War II]], the neighborhood was absorbed by the city of Mobile. A memorial bust of Lewis was placed in front of the historic Union Missionary Baptist Church.<ref name=SoulA/> The Africatown historic district was listed on the [[National Register of Historic Places listings in Mobile, Alabama|National Register of Historic Places]] in 2012. In May 2019, the [[Alabama Historical Commission]] announced that remnants of a ship found along the Mobile River, near 12 Mile Island and just north of the Mobile Bay delta, were confirmed as the ''Clotilda''.<ref name="keyes">{{cite web|url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smithsonian-institution/clotilda-last-known-slave-ship-arrive-us-found-180972177/|title=The 'Clotilda,' the Last Known Slave Ship to Arrive in the U.S., Is Found |last=Keyes|first=Allison|work=Smithsonian Magazine|date=22 May 2019|access-date=29 Jan 2021}}</ref> The wreck site was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2021.<ref>{{NRHPweekly}}</ref>

==History==
Captain William Foster was captain of the [[schooner]] ''Clotilda'',<ref name="garcia">[https://www.nytimes.com/2018/01/25/us/slave-ship-alabama-descendants.html Sandra E. Garcia and Matthew Haag, "Descendants' Stories of a Slave Ship Drew Doubts. Now Some See Validation"], ''New York Times'', 26 January 2018; accessed 26 January 2018</ref> working for [[Timothy Meaher]], a wealthy [[Mobile, Alabama|Mobile]] shipyard owner and steamboat captain. In 1855<ref name="raines">[https://www.al.com/news/mobile/index.ssf/2018/01/alcom_reporter_may_have_found.html Ben Raines, "Wreck found by reporter may be last American slave ship, archaeologists say"], AL.com, 25 January 2018; accessed 26 January 2018. Quote: "...the ship's license and the captain's journal make clear that Clotilda is correct." (as the name)</ref> or 1856,<ref name="foster" /> Meaher had built ''Clotilda'', a two-masted schooner {{convert|86|ft|m}} long with a beam of {{convert|23|ft|m}} and a [[Copper sheathing|copper-sheathed hull]], designed for the lumber trade.<ref name="raines1" />

The schooner had been refitted as a slave ship with a false deck. Foster obtained papers with the false claim he was delivering lumber. Disrupting the compass was 9,000 dollars in gold (containing magnetic metal impurities), which led the vessel off course. A hurricane off the Bermuda coast damaged the ship. While repairing, the crew of 11 who did not know the real mission purpose, discovered the hidden deck. To persuade them not to alert authorities, Foster agreed to pay them double, which ultimately he did not.<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=2018-05-07 |title=Zora Neale Hurston's Story of a Former Slave Finally Comes to Print |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2018/05/14/zora-neale-hurstons-story-of-a-former-slave-finally-comes-to-print |access-date=2023-02-09 |magazine=The New Yorker |language=en-US}}</ref>

Meaher had learned that [[West Africa]]n tribes were at war and that the [[King of Dahomey]] (now [[Benin]]) was willing to sell enemy prisoners as slaves. Dahomey's forces had been raiding communities in the interior, bringing captives to the large slave market at the port of Ouidah.<ref name="raines1" /><ref name="loc" /> Meaher was said to have wagered another wealthy gentleman from New Orleans,{{citation needed|date=May 2018}} that he could successfully smuggle Africans into the US despite the 1807 [[Act Prohibiting Importation of Slaves]].

Departing on March 4, 1860, Foster sailed from Mobile with a crew of 12, including himself,<ref name="foster">[https://digital.mobilepubliclibrary.org/items/show/1802 "Last Slaver from U.S. to Africa. A.D. 1860": Capt. William Foster, Journal of ''Clotilda''], 1860, ''Mobile Public Library Digital Collections''; accessed 28 January 2018</ref> arriving in Whydah on May 15, 1860,<ref name="foster" /> where he had the ship outfitted to carry Africans, using materials he had transported.<ref name="raines1" /> He offered to buy 125 Africans in [[Ouidah|Whydah]] for $100 each.<ref name="foster" /> said to be mostly of the "Tarkbar" tribe, taken in a raid near [[Tamale, Ghana|Tamale]] in present-day [[Ghana]].<ref name="loc">[http://memory.loc.gov/diglib/legacies/loc.afc.afc-legacies.200002671/ "AfricaTown, USA"], ''Local Legacies'', 2000, Library of Congress; accessed 28 January 2018</ref> Research in the 21st century suggests that they were actually Takpa or Tapa people, the northern [[Yoruba people|Yoruba]] name for the neighboring [[Nupe people|Nupe]] people from the interior of present-day [[Nigeria]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Dora Franklin Finley African-American Heritage Trail|url=https://www.dffaaht.org/|website=www.dffaaht.org|access-date=2020-05-21}}</ref>

He described meeting an African prince and being taken to the king's court, where he observed some religious practices. Foster wrote in his journal in 1860, "Having agreeably transacted affairs with the Prince we went to the warehouse where they had in confinement four thousand captives in a state of nudity from which they gave me liberty to select one hundred and twenty-five as mine offering to brand them for me, from which I preemptorily [sic] forbid; commenced taking on cargo of negroes, successfully securing on board one hundred and ten."<ref name="foster" />

As the captives were being loaded, Foster saw two steamers off the port and, fearing capture, ordered the crew to leave immediately, although only 110 Africans had been secured on board, leaving behind the last 15. They saw a [[Man-of-war|man o' war]] during the ocean passage, but escaped notice when a squall came up and they outran the ship,<ref name="foster" /> reaching Abaco lighthouse at the Bahama banks by June 30.<ref name="raines1" /> As they neared the United States, they disguised the schooner by taking down the "squaresail yards and the fore topmast", hoping to pass as a "coaster" carrying African captives within the US in the domestic [[Short sea shipping|coastal trade]].<ref name="foster" />

Foster's journal recorded that he anchored ''Clotilda'' on July 9 off Point of Pines in [[Grand Bay National Wildlife Refuge|Grand Bay]], Mississippi (likely referring to Point Aux Pins on Grand Bay in Alabama, near the Mississippi state line).  He traveled overland by horse and buggy to Mobile to meet with Meaher. Fearful of criminal charges, Captain Foster brought the schooner into the Port of Mobile at night and had it towed up the [[Spanish River (Alabama)|Spanish River]] to the [[Alabama River]] at [[Twelve Mile Island (Alabama River)|Twelve Mile Island]]. He transferred the African captives to a river steamboat, then burned ''Clotilda'' "to the water's edge" before sinking it.<ref name="foster"/> He paid off the crew and told them to return North.<ref name="foster"/>

The African captives were mostly distributed to the financial backers of the ''Clotilda'' venture, with Timothy Meaher retaining 30 captives on his property north of Mobile,<ref name=FerrisJMC/> including [[Cudjoe Lewis|Cudjo (aka Cudjoe) Lewis]], known as ''Kossoula'' or ''Kazoola''. Despite the racial hierarchy of the [[Deep South]], the Africans from ''Clotilda'' could not be legally registered as slaves because they were smuggled in; however, they were treated as [[Personal property|chattel]].<ref name=FerrisJMC/> Some of the captives were sold farther away, including [[Redoshi]] (later known also as Sally Smith) and a man later known as William or Billy, whom she was forced to marry on board the ship. They were sold to Washington Smith, a planter in [[Dallas County, Alabama]].<ref name="durkin" />

In 1861, the federal government prosecuted Meaher and Foster in Mobile for illegal slave importation, but the case was dismissed for lack of evidence from the ship or its manifest, and perhaps because of the outbreak of the [[American Civil War|Civil War]].

Because Captain Foster reported he burned and sank ''Clotilda''<ref name="SoulA" /> in the delta north of Mobile Bay, archaeological searches have continued into the 21st century for the wreck.<ref name=":0">{{cite web|url=https://news.nationalgeographic.com/2018/01/clotilda-slave-shipwreck-discovery-alabama-delta-spd/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180124234238/https://news.nationalgeographic.com/2018/01/clotilda-slave-shipwreck-discovery-alabama-delta-spd/|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 24, 2018|title=The Last Ship to Bring Slaves to the U.S. Has Not Been Found|author=Sarah Gibbens|publisher=National Geographic Society|date=Mar 6, 2018|access-date=Mar 12, 2018}}</ref> Several visible wrecks have been referred to by locals as the slave ship. Wreckage from ''Clotilda'' was allegedly found in 2018, but the Alabama Historical Commission ruled out the findings because of "major differences between the two vessels," and apparent lack of any fire damage.<ref name=":0" /> In May 2019, the Alabama Historical Commission announced the wreck had finally been found by researcher Ben Raines, showing "physical and forensic evidence [that] powerfully suggests that this is the Clotilda."<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.npr.org/2019/05/22/725900872/alabama-historians-say-the-last-known-slave-ship-has-been-found|title=Alabama Historians Say The Last Known Slave Ship To U.S. Has Been Found|newspaper=NPR|date=22 May 2019|language=en|access-date=2019-06-10|last1=Ingber|first1=Sasha}}</ref>

===Africatown===
{{main|Africatown}}
The Africans of the ''Clotilda'' were effectively emancipated at the end of the [[American Civil War|Civil War]]. As did many freedmen, Redoshi and William stayed with their daughter at the plantation in Bogue Chitto and continued to work there.<ref name="durkin"/>

Many of Meaher's former enslaved people returned to Magazine Point, and to land owned by Meaher on the [[Mobile-Tensaw River Delta]] just north of Mobile and on the west bank of the [[Mobile River]]. They founded the all-black community of [[Africatown]],<ref name="raines1"/> and attracted other ethnic Africans to join them in the independent community. They adopted community rules based on mostly "Takpa/Tapa" (Nupe) customs, and chose leaders. Some maintained the use of the [[Yoruba language]] and cultural traditions into the 1950s.<ref name="durkin"/>

Children born in the community began to learn English, first at church, and then in schools that were founded in the late nineteenth century. Cudjo Lewis lived until 1935 and was long thought to be the last survivor of the ''Clotilda''. In 2019, a new study established that Redoshi (Sally Smith) lived until 1937 in [[Bogue Chitto, Alabama|Bogue Chitto]], and she was thus considered the last survivor.<ref name="Durkin-2019">{{cite journal |last=Durkin |first=Hannah |title=Finding last middle passage survivor Sally 'Redoshi' Smith on the page and screen |journal=Slavery & Abolition |date=2019 |volume=40 |issue=4 |pages=631–658 |doi=10.1080/0144039X.2019.1596397|s2cid=150975893 }}</ref> But in 2020 it was announced that [[Matilda McCrear]] had survived until 1940, when she died in [[Selma, Alabama]].<ref name="Durkin 431–457"/>

The community of Africatown grew to 12,000 as new industry attracted workers to the upper river, including paper mills built after World War II. But with closing industries and job losses, the population has declined to about 2,000 in the early twenty-first century. In the postwar period, the area was mostly absorbed into a neighborhood of Mobile, with part in the neighboring town of [[Prichard, Alabama|Prichard]]. In 2012 the Africatown Historic District was recognized and listed on the [[National Register of Historic Places]]. Their cemetery is also listed.

== Finding the wreck ==
{{external media| float = right| video1 = [https://www.c-span.org/video/?517456-1/qa-ben-raines ''Q&A'' interview with Ben Raines on his book ''The Last Slave Ship: The True Story of How Clotilda Was Found, Her Descendants, and an Extraordinary Reckoning'', January 30, 2022], [[C-SPAN]]}} 
In January 2018, reporter Ben Raines identified what was originally believed to be the wreckage of the ''Clotilda'' in the lower [[Mobile–Tensaw River Delta|Mobile–Tensaw Delta]], a few miles north of the city of Mobile. Record low tides, caused by [[January 2018 North American blizzard|a storm system that produced a blizzard]], had left parts of a wreck visible above the mud.<ref name="garcia"/><ref name="raines1">{{Cite news|url=https://www.al.com/news/mobile/2018/01/alcom_reporter_may_have_found.html|title=Wreck found by reporter may be last American slave ship, archaeologists say|work=AL.com|access-date=2018-01-24|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/retropolis/wp/2018/01/24/the-last-u-s-slave-ship-was-burned-to-hide-its-horrors-a-storm-may-have-unearthed-it/|title=The last U.S. slave ship was burned to hide its horrors. A storm may have unearthed it.|last=Wootson|first=Cleve R. Jr.|date=2018-01-24|newspaper=Washington Post|access-date=2018-01-24|language=en-US|issn=0190-8286}}</ref> People in Africatown began to discuss what should be done with the wreckage if it was the ''Clotilda'', and how best to tell their story.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.npr.org/2019/05/22/725900872/alabama-historians-say-the-last-known-slave-ship-has-been-found | title=Alabama Historians Say The Last Known Slave Ship To U.S. Has Been Found | newspaper=NPR | date=May 22, 2019 | access-date=May 22, 2019 | author=Ingber, Sasha}}</ref>

However, by March 2018, researchers determined that the wreckage discovered by Raines was not ''Clotilda''.<ref name="raines2">{{Cite news|url=https://www.al.com/news/mobile/index.ssf/2018/03/wreck_found_in_delta_not_the_c.html|title=Wreck found in Delta not the Clotilda, the last American slave ship|work=AL.com|access-date=2018-03-05|language=en-US}}</ref> The [[National Park Service]] did designate the wreck that Raines discovered (of a ship almost twice as large as the ''Clotilda'') as the [[Twelvemile Island Ship Graveyard Historical and Archaeological District]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Twelvemile Island Shipwreck |url=https://www.nps.gov/articles/twelvemile-island-shipwreck.htm |website=NPS.gov |publisher=National Park Service |access-date=26 September 2023}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web| title=Report on a mid-to-late nineteenth-century wooden shipwreck in the east channel of the mobile river suggested as a candidate for the 1855 Schooner Clotilda, Baldwin county, Alabama | url=https://ahc.alabama.gov/PDF/Twelvemile%20Island%20Wreck_final_redacted%20version%205_28_19.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200811142320/https://ahc.alabama.gov/PDF/Twelvemile%20Island%20Wreck_final_redacted%20version%205_28_19.pdf | archive-date=2020-08-11}}</ref>

A few weeks later, Raines and a team from the [[University of Southern Mississippi]] returned to the river and performed the first survey of the 12 Mile Island section of the [[Mobile River]]. A week later, Raines and Monty Graham, head of Marine Sciences at the [[University of Southern Mississippi]], explored several of the 11 wrecks identified in the survey, along with Joe Turner and a team from Underwater Works Dive Shop. On April 13, Ben Raines pulled up the first piece of ''Clotilda'' to see the light of day in 160 years. The coordinates and survey data were shared with the Alabama Historical Commission, which hired Search Inc., to verify the find. The discovery was kept secret for a year, until the verification process was complete.

On May 22, 2019, the Alabama Historical Commission announced that the wreckage of the ''Clotilda'' had been found.<ref>{{cite news |last=Koplowitz |first=Howard |title=Clotilda, the last American slave ship, found in Alabama, historical commission says |url=https://www.al.com/news/2019/05/clotilda-the-last-american-slave-ship-has-been-found-alabama-historical-commission-announces.html |work=[[AL.com]] |access-date=May 22, 2019 |date=May 22, 2019 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Officials: Last slave ship from Africa ID'd on Alabama coast |url=https://www.fox10tv.com/news/officials-last-slave-ship-from-africa-id-d-on-alabama/article_cb085958-7cdb-11e9-b003-6ffb75cb8db3.html |work=[[WALA-TV]] |access-date=May 22, 2019 |date=May 22, 2019 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.npr.org/2019/05/22/725900872/alabama-historians-say-the-last-known-slave-ship-has-been-found | title=Alabama Historians Say The Last Known Slave Ship To U.S. Has Been Found | newspaper=NPR | date=22 May 2019 | access-date=22 May 2019 | author=Ingber, Sasha}}</ref>

==Representation in media==
The ''Clotilda'' has been frequently portrayed in the media. [[Margaret Brown (film director)|Margaret Brown]]'s 2008 documentary film ''[[The Order of Myths]]'' revealed that the queens of the two major, segregated [[Mardi Gras in Mobile, Alabama|Mardi Gras]] organizations in 2007 had a poignant link: the ancestors of the MCA queen had smuggled the ancestors of the MAMGA queen into Mobile Bay as slaves on the ''Clotilda''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pbs.org/independentlens/orderofmyths/film.html|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120906200725/http://www.pbs.org/independentlens/orderofmyths/film.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 6, 2012|title=Independent Lens . THE ORDER OF MYTHS . The Film|website=www.pbs.org|access-date=2019-05-25}}</ref> Brown followed up in 2022 with ''[[Descendant (2022 film)|Descendant]]'', a documentary film that looks into the Africatown community today, including the environmental and societal inequities still present after 160 years,  and the impact the ''Clotilda'''s 2019 discovery had on the area. Produced by [[Netflix]], it premiered at the 2022 [[Sundance Film Festival]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Daniels |first1=Robert |title='Descendant' Review: Africatown Documentary Rectifies Black Erasure by Filling Historical Gaps |url=https://www.indiewire.com/2022/01/descendant-review-africatown-documentary-1234692929/ |website=IndieWire |access-date=25 January 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Descendant review – powerful Netflix documentary on the legacy of slavery. A striking and sensitive film about how an illegal slave ship led to an Alabama community of inherited trauma but also defiance|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2022/oct/21/descendant-review-netflix-documentary-slavery|date=Oct 21, 2022|first=Lauren|last=Mechling}}</ref><ref>{{cite news
|title="The existence of the last slave transport ship was denied. A new documentary reveals the truth."|newspaper=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]|first=Alissa |last=Wilkinson|date=October 24, 2022 |url=https://www.vox.com/culture/23413296/descendant-netflix-clotilda-interview |access-date=October 30, 2022}}</ref> [[Henry Louis Gates Jr.]]'s ''[[Finding Your Roots]]'', Season 4, Episode 9 (December 12, 2017), showed census data for Mobile, and Captain William Foster's journal from the ''Clotilda'', during a segment explaining the family history of [[Questlove]], a drummer and music producer, joint frontman of the hip hop group [[The Roots]]. His great-great-great-grandparents Charles Lewis (born c. 1820) and his wife Maggie (born 1830) were among the slaves brought from West Africa on the ''Clotilda''. Gates found an article in ''[[The Pittsburgh Post]]'' of April 15, 1894 recounting the wager that Captain Timothy Meaher had made in 1859 that he could smuggle in slaves within two years,<ref>{{cite news|last=Boyd|first=Jared|date=December 18, 2017|title=PBS show reveals Questlove descended from last known slave ship, which landed in Alabama|newspaper=[[The Birmingham News]]|url=https://www.al.com/news/mobile/index.ssf/2017/12/pbs_special_reveals_questlove.html|access-date=December 18, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|newspaper=The Pittsburgh Post|date=April 15, 1894|page=17|title=The Last Cargo|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/20674270/|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> and one from ''[[The Daily Southerner|The Tarboro Daily Southerner]]'' of July 14, 1860 that 110 Africans had arrived in Mobile on ''Clotilda''. 

In 2018, [[Zora Neale Hurston]]'s book ''[[Barracoon: The Story of the Last "Black Cargo"|Barracoon]]'' was published, after lacking a publisher since its completion in 1931. An account of Cudjo Lewis' life story, it also discusses her feelings as an African-American researcher interviewing and getting to know him. It is an example of a "testimonial text".<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last=Sexton|first=Genevieve|date=2003|title=The Last Witness: Testimony and Desire in Zora Neale Hurston's "Barracoon"|journal=Discourse|language=en|volume=25|issue=1|pages=189–210|doi=10.1353/dis.2004.0012|s2cid=144347635|issn=1536-1810}}</ref> The song "Clotilda's on Fire," on [[Shemekia Copeland]]'s 2020 album ''Uncivil War'', deals with the vessel and her human cargo.<ref>{{cite news|title=On 'Uncivil War,' Shemekia Copeland Sets Fire To A Relic Of American Slavery|newspaper=[[NPR]]|first=Debbie|last=Elliott|date=November 2, 2020| url=https://www.ijpr.org/jpr-music/2020-11-02/on-uncivil-war-shemekia-copeland-sets-fire-to-a-relic-of-american-slavery| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201202072042/https://www.ijpr.org/jpr-music/2020-11-02/on-uncivil-war-shemekia-copeland-sets-fire-to-a-relic-of-american-slavery| url-status=usurped| archive-date=December 2, 2020|access-date=November 3, 2020}}</ref>
